title: Recurrent midgut volvulus in an adult patient — The case for pexy? A case report and review of the literature

segments.heading: Highlights
segments.text: • Intestinal malrotation and midgut volvulus in adulthood are rare events. • Reports of recurrence among adults are very scarce. The rate of recurrence and optimal surgical management are yet to be determined. • Bowel fixation procedures may be considered in Ladd procedures for adult midgut volvulus in order to reduce recurrence.

segments.heading: Abstract / Introduction
segments.text: Intestinal malrotation is a rare condition, with an incidence estimated between 0,2 to 1%. Most cases are diagnosed and treated during childhood. Adult presentations are rare and most adults present with chronic nonspecific complaints.

segments.heading: Abstract / Introduction
segments.text: Midgut volvulus is the most feared complication of intestinal malrotation, far more common among the pediatric than the adult population. Presentation in adulthood with a midgut volvulus accounts for a minority of these patients (15%).

segments.heading: Abstract / Introduction
segments.text: The Ladd procedure is the standard surgical management of midgut volvulus and intestinal malrotation. Most evidence on the outcomes of the Ladd procedure originates from studies on pediatric population and the recurrence among children who have had a Ladd procedure is low (2–7%).

segments.heading: Abstract / Presentation of case
segments.text: We report an exceedingly rare case of a patient who presented in adulthood with a midgut volvulus and less than two years after undergoing Ladd procedure presented with a recurrence of the midgut volvulus. The recurrent midgut volvulus was successfully treated by a fixation procedure (cecopexy and duodenopexy).

segments.heading: Abstract / Conclusion
segments.text: Reports of midgut volvulus in adult patients are scarce and reports of recurrence even scarcer hence the rate of recurrence among adult patients has yet to be determined. The recurrence rate in some of the available adult series is much higher than the rate reported among children.

segments.heading: Abstract / Conclusion
segments.text: Should the rate of recurrence among adult patients prove higher, it poses the question of whether the Ladd procedure should be modified to include bowel fixation when performed in adults.

segments.heading: Introduction
segments.text: Intestinal malrotation arises from a default in the intestinal rotation around the superior mesenteric artery that takes place during the normal embryonic development.

segments.heading: Introduction
segments.text: It is a rare event with a reported incidence ranging from 1/6000 to 1/200 (0.5%) of live births and 1% in autopsy studies [,].

segments.heading: Introduction
segments.text: Congenital intestinal malrotation is commonly diagnosed during childhood: an estimated 90% of patients are diagnosed during the first year of life [,] and adult presentations are rare and reported to account for only 0.2-0.5% of intestinal malrotation cases [, , , ]. Adult presentations are most commonly either incidental findings on radiological studies or chronic non-specific complaints such as abdominal pain or intermittent episodes of bowel obstruction. Only a minority of adult malrotation cases present with midgut volvulus [, , , ].

segments.heading: Introduction
segments.text: In a cohort of 82 adult patients Nehra et al. reported the most common complaints to be abdominal pain (present in 87% of patients), emesis (present in 37% of patients) and nausea (present in 31% of patients). Although only an estimated 15% of adults with malrotation present with midgut volvulus, it is the most worrisome complication of intestinal malrotation: in the absence of timely diagnosis a midgut volvulus may have catastrophic consequences with progression to gangrene of the rotated gut, sepsis and the need for extensive small bowel resection with subsequent short bowel syndrome [,,].

segments.heading: Introduction
segments.text: The surgical treatment of intestinal malrotation in children was described by Willian Ladd in 1936. The Ladd procedure consists of counter clockwise detorsion of the volvulus, division of all bands and adhesions securing the duodenum and bowel in abnormal position (the so-called ‘Ladd bands’), widening of the small bowel mesentery with repositioning of the duodenum and jejunum towards the right quadrant and repositioning of the colon towards the left side and appendectomy as the cecum will be positioned on the left [].

segments.heading: Introduction
segments.text: Recurrence of midgut volvulus after a Ladd procedure during childhood is a rare event [,]. Given the rarity of adult presentations of midgut volvulus, information on prognosis and reports of recurrence after Ladd procedure in adulthood are even more scarce.

segments.heading: Presentation of case
segments.text: A 22-year-old black male patient was admitted to the emergency department for non-specific abdominal pain. The patient described a periumbilical pain, lasting 12 h, worsened by food ingestion and he denied having nausea, emesis or changes in bowel habit. On further questioning the patient reported multiple episodes during his childhood of recurrent abdominal pain, occasionally accompanied by self-limited periods of bowel obstruction.

segments.heading: Presentation of case
segments.text: The patient had no relevant personal or family history. On physical examination he showed no signs of dehydration, vital signs were normal and he had no fever. Abdomen was soft, there was periumbilical tenderness but no signs of peritonitis. Blood tests were unremarkable, with a normal blood cell count and normal C-reactive protein.

segments.heading: Presentation of case
segments.text: Abdominal x-ray was non-specific, showing a decrease in bowel air content (Fig. 1).
segments.text_with_reference_markers: Abdominal x-ray was non-specific, showing a decrease in bowel air content ( [FIG:fig0005 Fig. 1] ).

segments.heading: Presentation of case
segments.text: Abdominal ultrasound showed the hallmark whirlpool sign [] of superior mesenteric vessels torsion; marked gastric distention and no free fluid (Fig. 2).
segments.text_with_reference_markers: Abdominal ultrasound showed the hallmark whirlpool sign [ [BIBR:bib0075 15] ] of superior mesenteric vessels torsion; marked gastric distention and no free fluid ( [FIG:fig0010 Fig. 2] ).

segments.heading: Presentation of case
segments.text: A diagnosis of acute midgut volvulus was established and an intravenous contrast CT scan was performed for further characterization of the malrotation. The CT showed aberrant distribution of bowel loops with the colon located on the left side and small bowel loops on the right side of the abdomen and torsion and dilation of the superior mesenteric vessels (Fig. 3).

The CT showed aberrant distribution of bowel loops with the colon located on the left side and small bowel loops on the right side of the abdomen and torsion and dilation of the superior mesenteric vessels ( [FIG:fig0015 Fig. 3] ).

segments.heading: Presentation of case
segments.text: The patient underwent urgent laparotomy with intra-operative confirmation of midgut volvulus due to intestinal malrotation. A Ladd procedure was performed: detorsion of the volvulus, division of ‘Ladd bands’, widening of the small bowel mesentery, repositioning of the duodenum and jejunum towards the right quadrant and the colon towards the left side and appendectomy (Fig. 4A–C).

A Ladd procedure was performed: detorsion of the volvulus, division of ‘Ladd bands’, widening of the small bowel mesentery, repositioning of the duodenum and jejunum towards the right quadrant and the colon towards the left side and appendectomy ( [FIG:fig0020 Fig. 4] A–C).

segments.heading: Presentation of case
segments.text: Post-operative course was uneventful.

segments.heading: Presentation of case
segments.text: Two years after the Ladd procedure the patient was re-admitted for acute abdominal pain with 48 h of duration, he denied nausea, emesis, or fever.

segments.heading: Presentation of case
segments.text: On physical examination the abdomen was distended, tympanic, bowel sounds were diminished and there was tenderness on palpation.

segments.heading: Presentation of case
segments.text: Blood tests were positive only for an increase in white blood cell count.

segments.heading: Presentation of case
segments.text: CT scan showed some free fluid, distended jejunal and ileal bowel loops and a collapsed colon with no identifiable transition point. There was no evidence of midgut volvulus recurrence.

segments.heading: Presentation of case
segments.text: Due to the worrisome findings of tenderness on physical examination, elevated white blood cell count and free fluid on the CT scan a decision was made to operate. The patient underwent a laparotomy and a recurrence of the midgut volvulus around the mesenteric axis was found. Following lysis of adhesions, the bowel rotation was reduced and a colopexy of the cecum to the left gutter was performed along with a pexy of the jejunum in the right gutter. Post-operative course was uneventful. At 3 years of follow-up since the second procedure, the patient has had no other events or symptoms.

segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: Recurrence of midgut volvulus after a childhood Ladd’s procedure is rare, reported to be between 2% and 7% [,,].

segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: Given the lower incidence of adult midgut volvulus (there are about 120 case reports and another 200 patients reported in 14 case series in the literature) the recurrence rate among adult patients is harder to estimate [,, , , , , ,, , , , , , , ].

segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: The best available evidence among children places the recurrence rate at 1.4%–3.5% (for open and laparoscopic Ladd procedure, respectively) [,,,, , , ]. The rate of recurrence among patients who underwent Ladd’s procedure in adulthood in some of the series is much higher than that reported in children with a recurrence rate as high as 16% [] and 18% [] in some series.

The rate of recurrence among patients who underwent Ladd’s procedure in adulthood in some of the series is much higher than that reported in children with a recurrence rate as high as 16% [ [BIBR:bib0085 17] ] and 18% [ [BIBR:bib0050 10] ] in some series.

segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: To the best of our knowledge, ours is the 9th case to be reported in the literature of adult recurrence of midgut volvulus after Ladd’s procedure during adulthood. Sheik and Alkan’s cases were not included as their cases report recurrence in adults that had a Ladd procedure in childhood [, , , , , ,, , , , , , , ,,].

segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: No high-level evidence is available to support management decisions on adult intestinal malrotation and volvulus. Moreover, it should be noted that while the literature significantly overlaps adult intestinal malrotation and midgut volvulus these are two different presentations of the same condition with different symptoms, severity and optimal management. It is questionable that data on adult intestinal malrotation should be the grounds for surgical management of adult midgut volvulus. The debate is still ongoing as to whether asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic (usually an incidental finding) intestinal malrotation warrants surgical treatment in adults [,,,, , ].

segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: The question of whether performing a fixation (pexy) of the abnormally positioned bowel segments diminishes the incidence of subsequent complications after Ladd procedure is long standing. Alexander Bill modified Ladd procedure in 1966 adding a suture of the posterior duodenum to the right renal fascia and a suture of the cecum to the left abdominal wall, arguing that this fixation would decrease recurrence of the midgut volvulus. In the 1980’s Stauffer [] reported a series of 77 children who had underwent either a Ladd procedure or Ladd procedure plus fixation and found a trend for less reoperation in the group with pexy but no significant difference in the recurrence rate among the two groups [,].

Alexander Bill modified Ladd procedure in 1966 adding a suture of the posterior duodenum to the right renal fascia and a suture of the cecum to the left abdominal wall, arguing that this fixation would decrease recurrence of the midgut volvulus. In the 1980’s Stauffer [ [BIBR:bib0170 34] ] reported a series of 77 children who had underwent either a Ladd procedure or Ladd procedure plus fixation and found a trend for less reoperation in the group with pexy but no significant difference in the recurrence rate among the two groups [ [BIBR:bib0170 34] , [BIBR:bib0175 35] ].

segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: Stauffer’s case series remains isolated as the highest quality available evidence on the matter, and while textbook and review authors [,] do not recommend a fixation procedure be added, a review of the available case series [,,,] shows that it is not uncommon practice to add a fixation procedure and it does constitute a safe option. Other options including the far more complex Fitzgerald and Wangensteen procedure have also been reported [].

Other options including the far more complex Fitzgerald and Wangensteen procedure have also been reported [ [BIBR:bib0190 38] ].

segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: As among children the recurrence rate is low, the pexy may constitute an unnecessary procedure. It should perhaps be considered when performing Ladd procedure in adult patients where, with a low morbidity and mortality risk, it may have the potential to lower recurrence of midgut volvulus.

segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: Durkin et al. had previously pointed out that the rate of reoperation increases the later a child is operated on [].

segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: One can hypothesize that adult patients, with a longer course of disease, may have more dramatic fibrotic changes in the mesentery making them more prone to a recurrence of the midgut volvulus around the mesenteric axis and it poses the question of whether additional gestures should be performed in the event of an adult Ladd procedure.

segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: After recurrence of the midgut volvulus in our patient, we chose to perform a pexy of the small and large bowel in an attempt to avoid recurrence. At 3 years of follow-up since the last procedure, the patient’s course has been uneventful.

segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: Further studies are necessary to establish the true incidence of recurrence of adult midgut volvulus and to define with a higher level of evidence its optimal management. The rarity of these cases may never allow for a definite answer though.

segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: Another rather rare aspect of our case report worth emphasizing is that the patient initially presented acutely with a midgut volvulus and while emesis and intermittent abdominal obstruction would prompt the alert pediatric surgeon to consider midgut volvulus these symptoms may well be underrated in an adult patient and lead to a late diagnosis after bowel ischemia has settled in.

segments.heading: Discussion
segments.text: Finally, it should be noted that as with all patients with a personal history of laparotomy, small bowel adhesions are the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in patients who have previously undergone a Ladd procedure []. However, given the dramatic consequences of a missed diagnosis of recurrence of midgut volvulus, this diagnosis should be firmly excluded before non-operative management of small bowel adhesions is undertaken.

segments.text: As with all cases of intestinal obstruction, tenderness on physical examination, lab results positive for systemic inflammation or persistence of symptoms after nasogastric tube decompression should result in a low threshold for operative management.

segments.heading: Conclusion
segments.text: Midgut volvulus is a potentially catastrophic consequence of intestinal malrotation. With most cases diagnosed and surgically corrected during childhood, the incidental diagnosis of intestinal malrotation or the acute diagnosis of midgut volvulus in the adult are rare events.

segments.heading: Conclusion
segments.text: The surgical management of midgut volvulus consists in the Ladd procedure. Recurrence of midgut volvulus among children who have had such procedure is low and the most common cause of intestinal obstruction among these patients is small bowel adhesions.

segments.heading: Conclusion
segments.text: The low incidence of midgut volvulus among adults results in a lack of data on the outcomes of an adult Ladd procedure. While recurrence seems to be an exceedingly rare complication of an already rare procedure, the recurrence rate for adult Ladd procedure derived from the scarce available data suggests it may be higher than that reported among children. This finding raises the question of whether the Ladd procedure performed in adults should be modified to include bowel fixation.

text:
[b00001] Highlights
• Intestinal malrotation and midgut volvulus in adulthood are rare events. • Reports of recurrence among adults are very scarce. The rate of recurrence and optimal surgical management are yet to be determined. • Bowel fixation procedures may be considered in Ladd procedures for adult midgut volvulus in order to reduce recurrence.

[b00002] Abstract / Introduction
Intestinal malrotation is a rare condition, with an incidence estimated between 0,2 to 1%. Most cases are diagnosed and treated during childhood. Adult presentations are rare and most adults present with chronic nonspecific complaints.

[b00003] Abstract / Introduction
Midgut volvulus is the most feared complication of intestinal malrotation, far more common among the pediatric than the adult population. Presentation in adulthood with a midgut volvulus accounts for a minority of these patients (15%).

[b00004] Abstract / Introduction
The Ladd procedure is the standard surgical management of midgut volvulus and intestinal malrotation. Most evidence on the outcomes of the Ladd procedure originates from studies on pediatric population and the recurrence among children who have had a Ladd procedure is low (2–7%).

[b00005] Abstract / Presentation of case
We report an exceedingly rare case of a patient who presented in adulthood with a midgut volvulus and less than two years after undergoing Ladd procedure presented with a recurrence of the midgut volvulus. The recurrent midgut volvulus was successfully treated by a fixation procedure (cecopexy and duodenopexy).

[b00006] Abstract / Conclusion
Reports of midgut volvulus in adult patients are scarce and reports of recurrence even scarcer hence the rate of recurrence among adult patients has yet to be determined. The recurrence rate in some of the available adult series is much higher than the rate reported among children.

[b00007] Abstract / Conclusion
Should the rate of recurrence among adult patients prove higher, it poses the question of whether the Ladd procedure should be modified to include bowel fixation when performed in adults.

[b00008] Introduction
Intestinal malrotation arises from a default in the intestinal rotation around the superior mesenteric artery that takes place during the normal embryonic development.

[b00009] Introduction
It is a rare event with a reported incidence ranging from 1/6000 to 1/200 (0.5%) of live births and 1% in autopsy studies [,].

[b00010] Introduction
Congenital intestinal malrotation is commonly diagnosed during childhood: an estimated 90% of patients are diagnosed during the first year of life [,] and adult presentations are rare and reported to account for only 0.2-0.5% of intestinal malrotation cases [, , , ]. Adult presentations are most commonly either incidental findings on radiological studies or chronic non-specific complaints such as abdominal pain or intermittent episodes of bowel obstruction. Only a minority of adult malrotation cases present with midgut volvulus [, , , ].

[b00011] Introduction
Among patients presenting with chronic complaints, the episodes are typically recurrent bouts of abdominal pain, which may be associated with nausea, vomiting, constipation or diarrhea. Such bouts have often been present since childhood [, , , ].

[b00012] Introduction
In a cohort of 82 adult patients Nehra et al. reported the most common complaints to be abdominal pain (present in 87% of patients), emesis (present in 37% of patients) and nausea (present in 31% of patients). Although only an estimated 15% of adults with malrotation present with midgut volvulus, it is the most worrisome complication of intestinal malrotation: in the absence of timely diagnosis a midgut volvulus may have catastrophic consequences with progression to gangrene of the rotated gut, sepsis and the need for extensive small bowel resection with subsequent short bowel syndrome [,,].

[b00013] Introduction
The surgical treatment of intestinal malrotation in children was described by Willian Ladd in 1936. The Ladd procedure consists of counter clockwise detorsion of the volvulus, division of all bands and adhesions securing the duodenum and bowel in abnormal position (the so-called ‘Ladd bands’), widening of the small bowel mesentery with repositioning of the duodenum and jejunum towards the right quadrant and repositioning of the colon towards the left side and appendectomy as the cecum will be positioned on the left [].

[b00014] Introduction
Recurrence of midgut volvulus after a Ladd procedure during childhood is a rare event [,]. Given the rarity of adult presentations of midgut volvulus, information on prognosis and reports of recurrence after Ladd procedure in adulthood are even more scarce.

[b00015] Introduction
This work is reported according to the SCARE 2018 criteria [].

[b00016] Presentation of case
A 22-year-old black male patient was admitted to the emergency department for non-specific abdominal pain. The patient described a periumbilical pain, lasting 12 h, worsened by food ingestion and he denied having nausea, emesis or changes in bowel habit. On further questioning the patient reported multiple episodes during his childhood of recurrent abdominal pain, occasionally accompanied by self-limited periods of bowel obstruction.

[b00017] Presentation of case
The patient had no relevant personal or family history. On physical examination he showed no signs of dehydration, vital signs were normal and he had no fever. Abdomen was soft, there was periumbilical tenderness but no signs of peritonitis. Blood tests were unremarkable, with a normal blood cell count and normal C-reactive protein.

[b00018] Presentation of case
Abdominal x-ray was non-specific, showing a decrease in bowel air content (Fig. 1).

[b00019] Presentation of case
Abdominal ultrasound showed the hallmark whirlpool sign [] of superior mesenteric vessels torsion; marked gastric distention and no free fluid (Fig. 2).

[b00020] Presentation of case
A diagnosis of acute midgut volvulus was established and an intravenous contrast CT scan was performed for further characterization of the malrotation. The CT showed aberrant distribution of bowel loops with the colon located on the left side and small bowel loops on the right side of the abdomen and torsion and dilation of the superior mesenteric vessels (Fig. 3).

[b00021] Presentation of case
The patient underwent urgent laparotomy with intra-operative confirmation of midgut volvulus due to intestinal malrotation. A Ladd procedure was performed: detorsion of the volvulus, division of ‘Ladd bands’, widening of the small bowel mesentery, repositioning of the duodenum and jejunum towards the right quadrant and the colon towards the left side and appendectomy (Fig. 4A–C).

[b00022] Presentation of case
Post-operative course was uneventful.

[b00023] Presentation of case
Two years after the Ladd procedure the patient was re-admitted for acute abdominal pain with 48 h of duration, he denied nausea, emesis, or fever.

[b00024] Presentation of case
On physical examination the abdomen was distended, tympanic, bowel sounds were diminished and there was tenderness on palpation.

[b00025] Presentation of case
Blood tests were positive only for an increase in white blood cell count.

[b00026] Presentation of case
CT scan showed some free fluid, distended jejunal and ileal bowel loops and a collapsed colon with no identifiable transition point. There was no evidence of midgut volvulus recurrence.

[b00027] Presentation of case
Due to the worrisome findings of tenderness on physical examination, elevated white blood cell count and free fluid on the CT scan a decision was made to operate. The patient underwent a laparotomy and a recurrence of the midgut volvulus around the mesenteric axis was found. Following lysis of adhesions, the bowel rotation was reduced and a colopexy of the cecum to the left gutter was performed along with a pexy of the jejunum in the right gutter. Post-operative course was uneventful. At 3 years of follow-up since the second procedure, the patient has had no other events or symptoms.

[b00028] Discussion
Recurrence of midgut volvulus after a childhood Ladd’s procedure is rare, reported to be between 2% and 7% [,,].

[b00029] Discussion
Given the lower incidence of adult midgut volvulus (there are about 120 case reports and another 200 patients reported in 14 case series in the literature) the recurrence rate among adult patients is harder to estimate [,, , , , , ,, , , , , , , ].

[b00030] Discussion
Table 1 presents a review of the reported case series of adult Ladd procedures. The series are small and heterogeneous including both intestinal malrotation and midgut volvulus cases and they vary widely in follow-up period.

[b00046] Discussion
The best available evidence among children places the recurrence rate at 1.4%–3.5% (for open and laparoscopic Ladd procedure, respectively) [,,,, , , ]. The rate of recurrence among patients who underwent Ladd’s procedure in adulthood in some of the series is much higher than that reported in children with a recurrence rate as high as 16% [] and 18% [] in some series.

[b00047] Discussion
To the best of our knowledge, ours is the 9th case to be reported in the literature of adult recurrence of midgut volvulus after Ladd’s procedure during adulthood. Sheik and Alkan’s cases were not included as their cases report recurrence in adults that had a Ladd procedure in childhood [, , , , , ,, , , , , , , ,,].

[b00048] Discussion
No high-level evidence is available to support management decisions on adult intestinal malrotation and volvulus. Moreover, it should be noted that while the literature significantly overlaps adult intestinal malrotation and midgut volvulus these are two different presentations of the same condition with different symptoms, severity and optimal management. It is questionable that data on adult intestinal malrotation should be the grounds for surgical management of adult midgut volvulus. The debate is still ongoing as to whether asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic (usually an incidental finding) intestinal malrotation warrants surgical treatment in adults [,,,, , ].

[b00049] Discussion
The question of whether performing a fixation (pexy) of the abnormally positioned bowel segments diminishes the incidence of subsequent complications after Ladd procedure is long standing. Alexander Bill modified Ladd procedure in 1966 adding a suture of the posterior duodenum to the right renal fascia and a suture of the cecum to the left abdominal wall, arguing that this fixation would decrease recurrence of the midgut volvulus. In the 1980’s Stauffer [] reported a series of 77 children who had underwent either a Ladd procedure or Ladd procedure plus fixation and found a trend for less reoperation in the group with pexy but no significant difference in the recurrence rate among the two groups [,].

[b00050] Discussion
Stauffer’s case series remains isolated as the highest quality available evidence on the matter, and while textbook and review authors [,] do not recommend a fixation procedure be added, a review of the available case series [,,,] shows that it is not uncommon practice to add a fixation procedure and it does constitute a safe option. Other options including the far more complex Fitzgerald and Wangensteen procedure have also been reported [].

[b00051] Discussion
As among children the recurrence rate is low, the pexy may constitute an unnecessary procedure. It should perhaps be considered when performing Ladd procedure in adult patients where, with a low morbidity and mortality risk, it may have the potential to lower recurrence of midgut volvulus.

[b00052] Discussion
Durkin et al. had previously pointed out that the rate of reoperation increases the later a child is operated on [].

[b00053] Discussion
One can hypothesize that adult patients, with a longer course of disease, may have more dramatic fibrotic changes in the mesentery making them more prone to a recurrence of the midgut volvulus around the mesenteric axis and it poses the question of whether additional gestures should be performed in the event of an adult Ladd procedure.

[b00054] Discussion
After recurrence of the midgut volvulus in our patient, we chose to perform a pexy of the small and large bowel in an attempt to avoid recurrence. At 3 years of follow-up since the last procedure, the patient’s course has been uneventful.

[b00055] Discussion
Further studies are necessary to establish the true incidence of recurrence of adult midgut volvulus and to define with a higher level of evidence its optimal management. The rarity of these cases may never allow for a definite answer though.

[b00056] Discussion
Another rather rare aspect of our case report worth emphasizing is that the patient initially presented acutely with a midgut volvulus and while emesis and intermittent abdominal obstruction would prompt the alert pediatric surgeon to consider midgut volvulus these symptoms may well be underrated in an adult patient and lead to a late diagnosis after bowel ischemia has settled in.

[b00057] Discussion
Finally, it should be noted that as with all patients with a personal history of laparotomy, small bowel adhesions are the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in patients who have previously undergone a Ladd procedure []. However, given the dramatic consequences of a missed diagnosis of recurrence of midgut volvulus, this diagnosis should be firmly excluded before non-operative management of small bowel adhesions is undertaken.

[b00058] Discussion
As with all cases of intestinal obstruction, tenderness on physical examination, lab results positive for systemic inflammation or persistence of symptoms after nasogastric tube decompression should result in a low threshold for operative management.

[b00059] Conclusion
Midgut volvulus is a potentially catastrophic consequence of intestinal malrotation. With most cases diagnosed and surgically corrected during childhood, the incidental diagnosis of intestinal malrotation or the acute diagnosis of midgut volvulus in the adult are rare events.

[b00060] Conclusion
The surgical management of midgut volvulus consists in the Ladd procedure. Recurrence of midgut volvulus among children who have had such procedure is low and the most common cause of intestinal obstruction among these patients is small bowel adhesions.

[b00061] Conclusion
The low incidence of midgut volvulus among adults results in a lack of data on the outcomes of an adult Ladd procedure. While recurrence seems to be an exceedingly rare complication of an already rare procedure, the recurrence rate for adult Ladd procedure derived from the scarce available data suggests it may be higher than that reported among children. This finding raises the question of whether the Ladd procedure performed in adults should be modified to include bowel fixation.
